La semaine dernière, plusieurs habitants: Last week, several Saint-Michel residents and community workers contacted us to tell us about the case of Abdellah Azzouz, a community worker at the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel who says he was a victim of racial profiling. He agreed to tell us his story.
Malheureusement, le SPVM n’a ni accepté: Unfortunately, the SPVM neither agreed to an interview nor confirmed or denied the facts. I was therefore unable to give the police a chance to speak.
Si vous avez vécu une expérience similai: If you have had a similar experience, or if you would like to suggest story ideas, don’t hesitate to write to me at <l1>loubna@laconverse.com</l1>
<strong>Abdellah Azzouz est intervenant: Abdellah Azzouz has been a community worker at the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel for three years. Having grown up in the Saint-Léonard neighbourhood of Montréal, he has always wanted to help others. Today, he shares with La Converse the account of a police stop he was subjected to and which he likens to racial profiling. His story.
Derrière son allure nonchalante, ses che: Behind his nonchalant air, his long, curly hair and his thick beard, Abdellah Azzouz radiates gentleness and serenity. He used to come to the Forum Jeunesse de Saint-Michel when he was younger, and is now a community worker there. It’s his way of “giving back.”
Malgré sa pudeur apparente, il a décidé: Despite his apparent reserve, he decided to speak out to denounce what he considers racial profiling. It all began on Thursday, October 10, around 10:45 p.m., while he was sitting in his parked vehicle.
« J’étais dans ma voiture, moteur à l’ar: “I was in my car, engine off, waiting for my friend,” he says. At that moment, he says he noticed a police car drive past him, then make a U-turn and stop next to his car. “A female officer gets out, comes over to me and asks me what I’m doing there. I told her I was waiting for my friend who lives right next door, to go get a coffee,” Abdellah Azzouz says. The officer then allegedly asked him if he was using any substances, to which the young man answered no.
Finalement, alors qu’il dit ne pas savoi: Finally, as he says he didn’t know why he was being stopped, she allegedly ordered him to state his identity. That’s when things took a completely different turn.
Selon Abdellah Azzouz, la policière a re: According to Abdellah Azzouz, the officer refused to tell him the reason for the stop, and a second officer allegedly arrived. “I wanted to know why I had to identify myself. Did I commit an offence? Is there any grounds at all for this stop? I just wanted an explanation, and I told her I would identify myself once I knew why I had to. But we had barely exchanged three sentences and her colleague arrived. He told me ‘enough talking’ and he opened the car door to pull me out,” recounts the community worker, who is of Algerian origin.
Une fois à bord de la voiture de police,: Once inside the police car, he says he explained that he is a community worker and works with the police to do prevention work with youth. “I told them that the week before, I had been in a meeting with the city’s mayor and that we had talked about the very problem of racial profiling in the Montréal police. When I said that, the officer replied: ‘too bad, you didn’t film anything.’ She meant that I had no proof, and she must know full well that the mayor has no authority over the police, even though the police answer to the City, which is their employer,” Abdellah Azzouz points out.
« Pour moi, j’ai subi ce contrôle simple: “For me, I was stopped simply because I look a certain way and I have long hair, the stereotype...” – Abdellah Azzouz
Finalement, il accepte de décliner son i: In the end, he agreed to state his identity to avoid being taken to the police station. “The officer took out a tablet with lots of photos and looked for mine. I told him I have a clean criminal record and have never had any trouble with the police. They ended up letting me go, but with a $500 fine for obstruction,” he explains, showing his ticket.
Abdellah Azzouz se dit choqué par cette: Abdellah Azzouz says he was shocked by the experience, as was his mother when she found out, and he quickly decided to share his story on his Facebook page. As a community worker whose role is to build bridges between Saint-Michel youth and the police, to work on preventing youth violence, and also to fight racial profiling, he says he felt a duty to speak out.
« Je sais bien que je n’ai pas de preuve: “I know very well that I don’t have proof, that I didn’t film it, but a lot of organizations, police officers and elected officials know me, invite me to events against violence and know that I’m serious. For me, I was stopped simply because I look a certain way and I have long hair, the stereotype... It’s an injustice and it’s not acceptable!” he insists.
Selon Abdellah Azzouz, l’équipe de polic: According to Abdellah Azzouz, the police team that carried out the stop belongs to the “Éclipse” section, which allegedly tends to engage in racial profiling. The website of the Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) states that the officers in this section have the mission to “fight crime and violence phenomena” and to “support, in the field, neighbourhood stations and the various investigative units in carrying out their intervention plans and investigative strategies.”
« Beaucoup de jeunes m’avaient raconté l: “Many young people had told me about their experiences with the Éclipse officers, and that they were fed up with being stopped all the time. I often asked them whether their attitude had been appropriate, whether they hadn’t done anything… but living it myself, when I was simply waiting for a friend, I realized that these are completely unjustified stops, based solely on our appearance, and that’s not normal,” says the community worker. He himself remembers an incident last June, when he was leaving a café with friends and was allegedly stopped by officers from the Éclipse section: “According to them, we had left the café too quickly. That makes no sense! That day, one officer recognized me and told her teammates that I worked with the city hall, so they didn’t continue the stop.”
Abdellah Azzouz l’assure, s’il témoigne: Abdellah Azzouz says that if he is speaking out today, it is to give a voice to neighbourhood youth who face racial profiling and who are “not believed.” He denounces the way the Éclipse section operates, and says relations are far more peaceful with officers from the neighbourhood stations, who know the area and its residents better.
« Ils sont tombés sur la mauvaise person: “They picked the wrong person, I want to take this as far as I can, because it’s an injustice.” – Abdellah Azzouz
Conscient que certaines personnes estime: Aware that some people think he should simply have identified himself, he maintains that he did not refuse to do so, but that it is “legitimate” to want to know why one is being stopped. He says the racial profiling of youth in Montréal’s neighbourhoods is also a financial issue. “Young people have told me they get stopped and given a ticket for supposedly crossing the street on a red light, and the police take the opportunity to search their phones. These are false pretexts, and they end up having problems with their parents, who think they did something to get stopped, and who end up paying a fine even though they’re already struggling financially. It’s no surprise that young people are afraid of the police,” the community worker says.
« Ils en ont marre de perdre 15-20 minut: “They’re fed up with losing 15 to 20 minutes every time they’re stopped for no reason. They’re fed up that the police only come to talk to them about negative things when they need to be given some recognition,” he says. According to the community worker, the SPVM must acknowledge these abuses and fight them firmly and concretely. He says he is in favour of officers wearing cameras during interventions: “It’s a solution that protects both the officers’ work and the public. It seems to me it would be very beneficial and easy to implement.”
Celui qui dit ne toujours pas savoir pou: He says he still doesn’t know why the officers decided to stop him that night, and he is determined to get an answer. “They picked the wrong person, I want to take this as far as I can, because it’s an injustice to be stopped without any explanation and to be taunted with ‘too bad you didn’t film anything,’” says Abdellah Azzouz. He hopes the police will cancel his fine, and says he will contest it if they don’t.
Tandis que la question du profilage raci: While the issue of racial profiling is getting more and more media attention, relatively little statistical data exists on the subject. In 2019, a first qualitative study conducted with a large sample of racialized youth in Montréal revealed that it is indeed a reality. Titled Les interpellations policières à la lumière des identités racisées des personnes interpellées, it was carried out by three Montréal academics, and their final report was submitted to the SPVM.
« Au cours de la période de quatre ans a: “Over the four-year period from 2014 to 2017, Black people were 4.2 times more likely to be stopped by the SPVM than white people, and Indigenous people were 4.6 times more likely to be stopped than white people. Arab people, for their part, were twice as likely to be stopped as white people,” the researchers note in their conclusions. Staggering figures.
« La Ville ne saurait se retrancher derr: “The City cannot hide behind its police officers or place the blame on them exclusively.” – Dominique Poulin, Superior Court judge.
Le rapport précise que « les interpellat: The report states that “stops of Arab and Black people are disproportionate, both in terms of their demographic weight in Montréal’s population and when considering their relative ‘contribution’ to municipal bylaw offences (over-stopping of 180% and 137% respectively for Arab and Black people) and to criminal offences (over-stopping of 93% and 66% respectively).”
Le 3 septembre dernier, au terme d’une a: On September 3, at the conclusion of a class action launched by Ligue des Noirs and Alexandre Lamontagne, a Montrealer who was a victim of profiling, the <l1>Superior Court</l1> found that SPVM officers were guilty of racial discrimination. Justice Dominique Poulin found the City of Montréal liable as the employer. “The City cannot hide behind its police officers or place the blame on them exclusively,” she said.
La juge accorde également aux personnes: The judge also awarded racialized people who were stopped without grounds between 2017 and 2019 between $2,500 and $5,000 in damages. Long awaited, the decision was welcomed by anti-racist activists, who see it as a “step forward,” even though it does not solve the underlying problem.
Contacté par La Converse au sujet du cas: Contacted by La Converse about Abdellah Azzouz’s case, the SPVM declined to comment. “The Service de police de la Ville de Montréal (SPVM) does not comment on specific police interventions, in order to prevent any influence on a possible judicial, ethics or disciplinary process. Except in rare cases, we also do not confirm specific arrests, or that a person – natural or legal – has filed or been the subject of a complaint, or that an investigation is being conducted,” the communications department told us.
De son côté, Abdellah Azzouz a pris rend: For his part, Abdellah Azzouz has made an appointment at the Saint-Michel legal clinic to learn about his rights and the options available to him. He says he is determined to continue his work to “keep young people from turning to crime,” while also standing up for “those who suffer in silence from racial profiling in Maghrebi and Black communities.”
Optimiste, il dit vouloir retrouver un l: Optimistic, he says he wants to rebuild a bond of trust between the police and young people. To that end, Abdellah Azzouz is considering entering politics in order to change things.
